title: At-Tariq: the night star
hookLine: by the sky and the piercing star, every soul has a guardian over it (86:1–4)

lines: THE ONE WHO COMES BY NIGHT.
cards: A knock on the door after midnight. The jolt, the heartbeat: who could that be? A knock at that hour usually means something.
Arabic has a single word for that visitor, the one who comes knocking by night. And the surah just before Al-A'la uses it for something in the sky.
A new stretch of the path starts here, the opening surahs of the thirtieth part, walked backward toward its first page. It starts with a knock. Today: At-Tariq, the night star.

teach.h: AT-TARIQ — THE ONE WHO KNOCKS BY NIGHT.
teach.b: Surah eighty-six begins: by the sky, and by at-tariq. The root t-r-q means to knock, to strike, and at-tariq is the one who comes knocking at night, a night visitor.
Then the surah asks, as it often does: and what will make you know what at-tariq is?

And answers: an-najm ath-thaqib, the piercing star, so bright it seems to punch a hole through the dark. Commentators have suggested different stars, and some say it means any bright star that appears at night.
The text doesn't name one. Then the point the oaths were leading to, verse four, in Pickthall's words: No human soul but hath a guardian over it.

teach.h: HAFIZ — ONE WHO KEEPS AND WATCHES.
teach.b: The word is hafiz, one who keeps, protects and watches. Commentators explain it as the angels Muslims believe are assigned to each person, some protecting, some recording what they do.
Others read it more broadly: God Himself keeps watch over every soul. Either way, the surah sets the two side by side. Up there in the dark, one bright point.
Down here, over every single person, something keeping watch too.
That ends a week: the orphan, again, then the soul at rest; the overwhelming, told in faces, and the camel worth a real look; the Most High, and the later that lasts. Now a star that knocks.
The surah goes on to say that the human being was made from water poured out, and that the One who made him can bring him back. That waits for the path's later years.

how: At-Tariq is among the short surahs many Muslims memorize and recite in prayer; its verse on every soul having a guardian is often recalled as a comfort, and Muslims believe angels are assigned to watch over and record each person.

practice: Think of the people you love who are far from you tonight: a parent, a child, a friend in another city. Picture each one, one at a time, with a small bright point above them, keeping watch. Then picture one over yourself.

wordCard.voice: At-Tariq. The night visitor, the piercing star, and the name of Surah eighty-six: every soul has a guardian over it. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: the night visitor, from t-r-q, to knock or strike; the name of Surah 86.

carryVoice: Your line: every soul has a guardian. Up there one bright point; down here, a watch kept over everyone. Another week behind you.
